meta.titre: Pressure Belts and Planetary Winds: from belts of rising and sinking air to wind directions
meta.sous_theme: World pressure belts, trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies

sections.contenu_markdown: In the dry season in northern Cameroon, a dusty wind from the Sahara can reduce visibility and dry out lips and skin. In the rainy season, damp air from the Atlantic brings storms. These changes belong to a world pattern of pressure belts and winds. The GCE paper asks you to name the winds, give their directions and draw the pattern in a labelled diagram, so you need both the facts and a method for drawing.

items: Warm air is lighter than cold air and tends to rise.
Latitude is measured in degrees north and south of the equator.
The Earth rotates from west to east, and the sun is overhead at the equator in March and September.
A wind is named after the direction it blows from.

sections.titre: The pressure belts and the winds that blow between them
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Pressure and wind
Air pressure is the weight of the air pressing on the surface. Rising air leaves low pressure at the ground; sinking air gives high pressure. **Wind is air moving from a high-pressure belt to a low-pressure belt.** The Earth's rotation bends moving air to the **right** in the Northern Hemisphere and to the **left** in the Southern Hemisphere.

### The four pressure belts
| Belt | Approximate latitude | Pressure | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equatorial low (doldrums) | 0° to 5° | Low | Strong heating makes air rise |
| Sub-tropical highs | about 30° N and S | High | Air that rose at the equator cools and sinks |
| Sub-polar (temperate) lows | about 60° N and S | Low | Warm air meets cold air and is forced to rise |
| Polar highs | 90° N and S | High | Very cold, dense air sinks |

### The three planetary winds
| Wind | Blows from, to | Northern Hemisphere | Southern Hemisphere |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trade winds | Sub-tropical highs to equatorial low | North-easterly | South-easterly |
| Westerlies | Sub-tropical highs to sub-polar lows | South-westerly | North-westerly |
| Polar easterlies | Polar highs to sub-polar lows | North-easterly | South-easterly |

### Seasonal shift
The belts follow the overhead sun, moving north in the northern summer and south in the southern summer. A place near the edge of a belt can therefore change wind and weather during the year. In Cameroon the dry, dusty north-east trade wind (the Harmattan) is felt mainly in the dry season, while moist air from the Atlantic arrives in the wet season.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question says draw or show the belts and winds
variantes.contenu_markdown: Draw a vertical line (or a half-circle) from the North Pole to the South Pole and mark 90° N, 60° N, 30° N, 0°, 30° S, 60° S and 90° S. Write **H** or **L** at each latitude with the belt name. Between the belts draw arrows in the correct direction, then label them with the wind names. Add a title. Marks are normally given for correct latitudes, belt names, wind arrows and wind names, and for neat labelling.

variantes.nom: Finding a wind direction in two steps
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must give the direction of a named wind
variantes.contenu_markdown: Step 1: draw the straight path from the high to the low. Step 2: bend it to the right in the north or to the left in the south. Example: in the Northern Hemisphere the trade winds first move south; bent to the right they move towards the south-west, so they are **north-easterly** winds (the name comes from where the wind blows from).

variantes.nom: Multiple-choice questions on belts and winds
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives two latitudes or a wind and asks for the other
variantes.contenu_markdown: Match the pair: 30° to the equator gives trade winds; 30° to 60° gives westerlies; 90° to 60° gives polar easterlies. Check the hemisphere before choosing the direction.

sections.enonce_markdown: Describe the planetary winds of the Northern Hemisphere and explain why they do not blow due north or due south. (6 marks)

etapes.action: List the three winds with their belts.
etapes.justification: The description needs each wind and the belts it connects.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Trade winds blow from about 30° N to the equator, westerlies from 30° N to 60° N, and polar easterlies from 90° N to 60° N.

etapes.justification: Direction must be stated using the compass point it comes from.

etapes.action: Name the cause of the bending.
etapes.justification: The explanation needs a reason, not only a description.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The Earth's rotation deflects moving air.

etapes.action: State the rule for the hemisphere.
etapes.justification: Examiners reward the direction of deflection.
etapes.resultat_markdown: In the Northern Hemisphere the deflection is to the right of the path.

etapes.action: Apply the rule to one wind.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Trade winds start moving south; bending to the right turns them towards the south-west, so they blow from the north-east.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer: In the Northern Hemisphere the trade winds blow from the sub-tropical high near 30° N towards the equatorial low as north-easterly winds. The westerlies blow from 30° N towards the sub-polar low near 60° N as south-westerly winds. The polar easterlies blow from the polar high towards the sub-polar low as north-easterly winds. The winds do not blow due north or south because the Earth's rotation deflects moving air. In the Northern Hemisphere the deflection is to the right, so a wind that starts moving south is turned towards the south-west and blows from the north-east.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that the trade winds are "south-westerly" in the Northern Hemisphere.
items.pourquoi_faux: A wind is named after the direction it comes from, and the northern trades come from the north-east.
items.correction_markdown: Write north-easterly for the northern trades and south-easterly for the southern trades.

items.erreur_markdown: Putting high pressure at the equator.
items.pourquoi_faux: Strong heating makes air rise at the equator, which gives low pressure.
items.correction_markdown: Label the equator L, the sub-tropics (about 30°) H, the sub-polar belts (about 60°) L and the poles H.

items.erreur_markdown: Drawing arrows from a low-pressure belt towards a high-pressure belt.
items.pourquoi_faux: Wind blows from high pressure to low pressure.
items.correction_markdown: Draw each arrow so that it starts at an H belt and ends at an L belt.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving the same deflection in both hemispheres.
items.pourquoi_faux: Winds turn to the right in the north and to the left in the south.
items.correction_markdown: Say right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere, then check the resulting direction.

items.erreur_markdown: Leaving out latitudes and a title on the diagram.
items.pourquoi_faux: Without latitudes and a title the examiner cannot credit the position of the belts.
items.correction_markdown: Mark 0°, 30°, 60° and 90° and give the diagram a title.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the wind that blows from the sub-tropical high near 30° S to the equatorial low, and give its direction.
items.solution_markdown: The wind blows from the sub-tropical high to the equatorial low, so it is a **trade wind**. In the Southern Hemisphere it moves north and is bent to the left, towards the north-west, so it blows from the south-east. Answer: **south-east trade wind**.

items.enonce_markdown: A sailing ship is carried by the trade winds from 30° N to the equator at an average speed of 15 km per hour. Taking 1° of latitude as 111 km, calculate the distance and the time taken, in days and hours.
items.solution_markdown:
Distance = 30 x 111 = **3330 km**.

Time = distance / speed = 3330 / 15 = **222 hours** = 9 days 6 hours (because 222 = 9 x 24 + 6).

Answer: **3330 km in 9 days 6 hours**.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain why the pressure belts move north and south during the year, and state one effect of this movement on the weather of a tropical place. (5 marks)
items.solution_markdown:
Award marks for the following points.
- The overhead sun moves between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn during the year.
- The belts of heating follow the sun, so the pressure belts and wind belts move north in the northern summer and south in the southern summer.
- Effect: when the equatorial low is overhead, a tropical place has rising air, cloud and rain; when the belt has moved away and the place lies under a high-pressure belt or dry trade winds, the weather is dry.

**The movement follows the overhead sun, and it changes tropical places between a wet season and a dry season.**

items_markdown: Wind blows from high pressure to low pressure and is bent right in the north and left in the south.
Belts: equatorial low (0°), sub-tropical highs (30°), sub-polar lows (60°), polar highs (90°).
Trade winds blow from the sub-tropical highs to the equator, westerlies from the sub-tropical highs to the sub-polar lows, and polar easterlies from the poles to the sub-polar lows.
A wind is named after the direction it comes from: northern trades are north-easterly and southern westerlies are north-westerly.
In a diagram give latitudes, belt names with H and L, labelled arrows and a title.
The belts follow the overhead sun, which explains wet and dry seasons in the tropics.
